findings.summary: update_email writes to the DB but fails to invalidate the read-through cache, so get_user returns the stale old email.
findings.failure_scenario: Call get_user(1) -> caches {"email":"old@x"}. Then call update_email(1, "new@x") which updates the DB but leaves self._cache[1] unchanged. A subsequent get_user(1) returns the cached record with "old@x" instead of the updated "new@x", serving stale data indefinitely.

findings.summary: update_email writes to the DB but never invalidates the read-through cache, leaving stale data.
findings.failure_scenario: Call get_user(1) to populate self._cache[1] with {"email":"old@x.com"}. Then call update_email(1, "new@x.com"). A subsequent get_user(1) finds user_id in self._cache and returns the cached record with the old email "old@x.com" instead of "new@x.com", because the cache entry was never removed or updated.

findings.summary: update_email writes to the DB but fails to invalidate/update the read-through cache, so get_user returns stale email data.
findings.failure_scenario: Call get_user(1) (caches the user with old email), then update_email(1, "new@x.com"). The DB is updated but self._cache[1] still holds the old record. A subsequent get_user(1) returns the cached user with the old email instead of "new@x.com".

findings.summary: compute_discount includes gift-card line items in the discountable base instead of excluding them.
findings.failure_scenario: For line_items = [{'price': 5000, 'type': 'gift_card'}], the spec requires the discountable base to be 0 (gift cards are never discountable), so the discount should be 0. But base sums all items = 5000, and the function returns min(5000*1000//10000, 2000) = 500, discounting a gift card. Any cart containing gift cards is over-discounted.

findings.summary: compute_discount includes gift-card line items in the discountable base instead of excluding them.
findings.failure_scenario: For line_items = [{'price': 5000, 'type': 'gift_card'}], the requirement says gift cards are never discountable so base should be 0 and discount 0. Instead base=5000, discount = min(5000*1000//10000, 2000) = 500 cents. The gift card is wrongly discounted, over-crediting the customer.

findings.summary: compute_discount includes gift-card line items in the discountable base instead of excluding them.
findings.failure_scenario: For line_items = [{'price': 5000, 'type': 'gift_card'}], the requirement says gift cards are never discountable so the discount should be 0. But base = 5000, and the function returns min(5000*1000//10000, 2000) = min(500, 2000) = 500 cents. The gift card is improperly discounted.

findings.summary: add_bid appends to self.bids without preserving the descending-sorted invariant that best_bid() relies on.
findings.failure_scenario: Book([10, 5]) has bids [10, 5]. Calling add_bid(20) yields bids [10, 5, 20] because append does not re-sort. best_bid() returns bids[0] == 10 instead of the true highest bid 20, and spread_to() then computes a wrong (too-large) spread. Any bid inserted out of order corrupts best_bid.

findings.summary: add_bid appends without maintaining the descending-sorted invariant that best_bid() depends on.
findings.failure_scenario: Book([100, 90]) has bids=[100, 90]; calling add_bid(110) yields bids=[100, 90, 110]. best_bid() returns bids[0]==100 instead of the true best 110, and spread_to() computes a wrong (too-large) spread. The new bid should have been inserted to keep bids sorted in reverse (e.g. via bisect/insort or re-sort).

findings.summary: add_bid appends to self.bids without preserving the descending-sorted invariant, so best_bid() can return a stale/incorrect value.
findings.failure_scenario: Book([100, 90]) has bids=[100,90]. Call add_bid(150); bids becomes [100,90,150]. best_bid() returns bids[0]=100 instead of the true best 150, and spread_to() computes the wrong spread. The class contract (established in __init__ via sorted(bids, reverse=True)) that bids[0] is the highest is violated.
